items.title: Prevalence of Arthritis in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus in Pakistan: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disease with diverse clinical manifestations that significantly affect patients' quality of life. Arthritis is one of the most common and disabling manifestations of SLE. This study aimed to provide a comprehensive estimate of the prevalence of arthritis among patients with SLE in Pakistan and to evaluate regional and temporal variations. Two independent reviewers selected eligible studies, extracted the data, and assessed the risk of bias. A random-effects meta-analysis was performed to account for between-study heterogeneity. Subgroup analyses and meta-regression were conducted to explore potential sources of study-level variation. A total of 10 studies involving 1,292 participants were included in the meta-analysis. The pooled prevalence of arthritis among patients with SLE was 60.68% (95% CI: 46.41%-74.08%). Subgroup analysis showed that the highest prevalence was observed in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) (78.13%; 95% CI: 74.83%-81.11%), followed by Punjab (58.94%; 95% CI: 38.19%-78.15%) and Sindh (57.28%; 95% CI: 29.43%-82.82%). Studies published after 2010 reported a higher pooled prevalence (67.89%; 95% CI: 54.47%-79.95%) than those published before 2010 (42.11%; 95% CI: 34.74%-49.67%). The high prevalence of arthritis among patients with SLE in Pakistan highlights the need for improved screening, early diagnosis, and effective management strategies to reduce disease burden and improve patient outcomes. This systematic review and meta-analysis was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42023420108) on May 1st, 2023.

items.title: Histone lactylation: a metabolic-epigenetic bridge linking glycolysis to salivary gland fibrosis in Sjögren's disease.
items.abstract: Sjögren's disease (SjD) is a chronic, systemic autoimmune disorder characterized by lymphocytic infiltration and progressive loss of exocrine gland function. Despite advances in understanding its immunopathogenesis, the molecular mechanisms governing the transition from inflammation to irreversible salivary gland fibrosis remain obscure. Emerging evidence suggests that the crosstalk between metabolic reprogramming and epigenetic modifications profoundly shapes the local inflammatory microenvironment and accelerates disease progression. Histone lactylation, a recently discovered lactate-derived epigenetic mark, directly couples enhanced glycolytic activity and lactate accumulation with transcriptional regulation, thereby serving as a pivotal metabolic-epigenetic bridge. This review systematically examines the potential role of histone lactylation in SjD salivary gland pathology. We delineate the enzymatic machinery of lactylation, the metabolic origins of lactate within the inflamed microenvironment, and the functional implications for immune cell polarization, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and myofibroblast activation. While direct evidence in SjD is currently lacking, we synthesize findings by integrating immunometabolism, epigenetic rewiring, and tissue fibrogenesis, we aim to establish histone lactylation as a transformative framework for understanding SjD pathogenesis and highlight its translational potential for novel biomarkers and therapeutic interventions.

items.title: Gut dysbiosis in difficult-to-treat rheumatoid arthritis: hypothesized microbial endotypes, persistent inflammation, and pharmacological treatment resistance.
items.abstract: Difficult-to-treat rheumatoid arthritis (D2T RA) remains a major clinical problem despite treat-to-target care and an expanding range of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs). D2T RA includes biologically distinct states, particularly persistent inflammatory refractory rheumatoid arthritis (PIRRA) and non-inflammatory refractory rheumatoid arthritis (NIRRA). Direct microbiome evidence in D2T RA is sparse, but studies in established RA, at-risk populations, and treatment-response cohorts suggest that intestinal ecological disruption may sustain inflammation through barrier failure, persistent microbial-product sensing, and impaired metabolite-mediated immune regulation. Gut microorganisms may also influence drug response, especially to methotrexate, while antirheumatic therapy can remodel the microbial ecosystem. We therefore synthesize the literature into three hypothesis-generating functional states, provisionally termed inflammation-amplifying, immune-tolerance-deficient, and poor-drug-response-associated microbial endotypes. These states are not validated patient classes and may overlap or evolve over time. We also propose a microbiota-treatment resistance feedback loop, explicitly as an inferential model rather than an established causal pathway. Microbiota-directed adjuncts are evaluated according to evidence maturity, mechanistic fit, and safety. Overall, the gut microbiota is best considered a potential upstream modifier linking mucosal immunity, persistent inflammation, and pharmacological response, with the most coherent mechanistic relevance to PIRRA. Prospective D2T RA cohorts with objective inflammatory phenotyping, longitudinal multi-omics, and detailed drug-exposure data are needed before these concepts can inform clinical stratification or treatment.

items.title: Comparative efficacy and safety of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs tapering strategies in sustained-remission rheumatoid arthritis: Systematic review and network meta-analysis.
items.abstract: International guidelines permit tapering disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in sustained remission, but the de-escalation strategy with the lowest risk of flare remains unknown. Therefore, this study aimed to compare and rank flare risk across DMARD de-escalation strategies to guide more specific clinical decisions. We performed a systematic review and a frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis (NMA) of clinical studies, evaluating DMARD tapering in adults with RA in remission (≥6 months). The primary network compared maintenance therapy (N0), simultaneous dose reduction of cDMARDs and bDMARDs (N1), discontinuation of bDMARDs while continuing cDMARDs (N3), and dose reduction of bDMARDs while continuing cDMARDs (N4). Flare risk was pooled as RR (95% CI) using a consistency model, with ranking by P-scores. Assessments of risk of bias, network inconsistency, and confidence in network estimates using CINeMA, as well as sensitivity analysis including complete DMARD withdrawal (N2), were also conducted. nineteen studies involving 3115 participants were included. Overall, tapering DMARDs increased the risk of flares compared with continued therapy (RR 1.94; 95%CI: 1.30-2.89). The primary NMA showed that tapering bDMARDs while continuing cDMARDs (N4) had the most favourable flare profile among the evaluated de-escalation strategies and was closest to maintenance therapy (RR 1.17; 95%CI: 0.76-1.82). In contrast, discontinuation of bDMARDs while continuing cDMARDs (N3) increased flare risk compared to N0 (RR 3.06; 95% CI: 1.81-5.16), and compared to N4 (RR 2.61; 95% CI: 1.44-4.72). The order of strategies identified was N0 > N4 > N1 > N3. CINeMA confidence was high for N3 versus N0 and moderate for N4 versus N0. Gradual bDMARD dose reduction while maintaining background cDMARD as backbone therapy showed the most favourable comparative flare profile, whereas bDMARD discontinuation was associated with a substantially higher flare risk.
